perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for this trauma profile. As a male firefighter whose index trauma is relief work in a war zone, moral-violation cues are plausible, but 'Babies' and especially 'Comments on sexual violence' imply highly specific trauma-linked content that is not supported anywhere else in the memory, threat, or appraisal items. Those other nodes describe moral injury, disorganized trauma memory, pain recall, anger, and global alienation, but contain no infant-related or sexual-violence-related material. This makes those two triggers feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation rather than part of the same trauma network.

issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Feelings' is internally contradictory in wording: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of emotional avoidance. It conflicts with the node label and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise suggests suppression/avoidance and control strategies in response to distress. This item is therefore not clinically coherent as selected.

issues.item: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: This item directly contradicts the Maladaptive Strategies construct and the rest of the profile. 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes openness to emotion rather than avoidance of feelings. It is internally inconsistent within the node, where the other items are clearly maladaptive avoidance/control strategies (self-harm to regulate affect, mental rituals to prevent recurrence), and it does not fit the cognitive formulation linking negative appraisals, memory, and threat to maladaptive coping.

vignette:
Bao presents as a 46-year-old man whose stoic demeanor seems to barely contain a profound and restless agitation. A firefighter with two decades of service, he describes the last eighteen months as a "slow-motion collapse" following his volunteer deployment as a relief worker in a war-torn region. It was there, amidst the rubble of a besieged city, that the event occurred. His unit was evacuating a partially collapsed apartment building when the sounds began-shrieks from an adjacent, inaccessible wing of the complex. They were under strict orders to hold their position. Bao remembers the commander's voice on the radio, sharp and absolute, but it's drowned out by the memory of the screams, which were not of pain, but of a particular kind of terror. Then, a deafening blast threw him against a wall. The world dissolved into dust and a searing, white-hot agony in his back and left leg.

The memories of that day do not return to him as a story. Instead, they come in jagged pieces, a sequence he can never seem to straighten out. Sometimes it's just the sound of the screams, other times it's the physical sensation of the impact, a phantom pain that shoots down his spine so intensely he has to brace himself against a wall. When he tries to explain it, the words fail him. He knows what he wants to say, the horror he wants to convey, but the vocabulary evaporates, leaving him with a frustrating, inarticulate silence. He has come to believe that the chaos of the event permanently scrambled his ability to make sense of it, not just for others, but for himself.

Back at his firehouse in the States, the familiar environment has become a landscape of hidden threats. The long, tense quiet in the truck on the way to a call feels menacing, a silence he is certain is about to be shattered by catastrophe. A car backfiring on the street, or the sudden whoosh and bang of a backdraft at a scene, can instantly transport him back to the explosion. In those moments, he feels the shrapnel in his back all over again. His crew, once his brothers, now give him a wide berth. His irritability has grown into a constant, simmering anger that boils over without warning, and his captain has formally warned him about his aggressive outbursts. He feels their distance as a judgment, confirming a belief that has taken root deep inside him: he no longer belongs anywhere. He is not one of them anymore.

At home in his empty apartment, the one he moved into after his wife left, he is haunted. A news report mentioning sexual violence will trigger the memory of the screams from the apartment wing, and with it, a wave of guilt so powerful it feels like a physical illness. He is certain he acted in a way that goes against everything he is supposed to be-a protector, a rescuer. He should have disobeyed orders. He should have done something. This thought loops endlessly, a self-inflicted torment. To manage these overwhelming feelings, he has developed his own painful rituals. He tries to forcefully suppress the thoughts, pushing them down until the pressure is unbearable. When that fails, he will dig his fingernails into the flesh of his arm, the sharp, grounding pain a temporary release from the emotional agony. Before every shift, he performs a sequence of silent actions-tapping his helmet three times, checking the latch on his door twice-a desperate, magical attempt to ensure nothing bad will happen to his crew, a responsibility he feels he catastrophically failed once before.

Bao sought therapy after his captain put him on administrative leave, telling him he couldn't return to active duty until he was "cleared." The ultimatum was both a humiliation and a lifeline. He feels his life has been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma, a permanent stain on his character. What frightens him most is the conviction that the man he was-the confident firefighter, the husband, the man who believed in his own moral courage-is gone forever, replaced by this angry, frightened stranger.
